research.query: How does soot form in microgravity flames?
research.answer:
The question was matched to: microgravity, soot. Below is what the indexed documents state about it, quoted with their sources.

**Evidence**
- Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets: A Combined Experimental and Computational Study of Soot Formation in Normal and Microgravity Conditions (2022) [S1]
- Computational and Experimental Analysis of SPICE Data Sets: Microgravity conditions would produce longer, more diffuse flames with lower temperatures and increased soot concentrations compared to normal gravity, and that careful integration of experimental temperature fields into the simulations would reduce discrepancies between… [S2]
- ACME CLD Flame: B) Characterize the sooting tendencies of diffusion flames with long residence times, as a function of velocity and fuel dilution, through measurement of flame shape, gas temperatures in the soot-free portion of the flame, soot luminosity, soot temperatures, and soot volume… [S3]
- SLICE: A computational and experimental study of coflow laminar methane/air diffusion flames: Effects of fuel dilution, inlet velocity, and gravity; A Combined Experimental and Computational Study of Soot Formation in Normal and Microgravity Conditions; Effects of Fuel Dilution and… [S4]
- FLEX-2: 4. Analyze the soot formation process, including soot volume fraction soot-shell dynamics. [S5]
- Dust can look like smoke to a particle counter: DAFT showed that a modified commercial particle counter could be used in microgravity, measuring a test dust aerosol released on the ISS. Limitation: Terrestrial test dust, not lunar regolith; feasibility test only. [S10]
- Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a f [S11]

**Limits**
- Extractive answer (no language model configured): passages are quoted, not interpreted.
- Only documents in this knowledge base were searched.

sources.title: ACME CLD Flame — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments / Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame — approach
sources.text: ACME CLD Flame project goals include the generation of improved computational models with improved soot sub-models that are effective for both dilute flames and sooting flames that vary from low to high soot loading levels. The enhanced time and spatial scales in a microgravity environment will be important for achieving both goals. Experimentally, we plan to study methane and ethylene diffusion flames over a wide range of test conditions. For the more dilute flames, measurements will be made of flame chemiluminesence of OH* and CH* to observe variations in lift-off height and flame shape as extinction limits are approached.

sources.title: Stopping ventilation may not be enough in oxygen-enriched cabins
sources.text: In quiescent microgravity, BRE flames emulating condensed materials (e.g. PMMA, nylon) kept burning quasi-steadily in the elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, whereas comparable flames at 21 % O2 self-extinguished in a short time. PSI describes these results as preliminary. Limitation: Gaseous emulation of solids; per-test pressure not in the summary table; results flagged preliminary.

top_passage.text: Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions. The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate, with special emphasis on reproducing the “Goldilocks” flammability zone reported by Olson and Ferkul. Comparative analyses were also carried out with a parallel NSF-supported terrestrial flame spread project, ensuring that the predictive capabilities of the UFGM approach were assessed across both microgravity and normal-gravity conditions.
